title: Data Catalogs & Metadata Management
summary: A dataset nobody can find or trust is functionally unavailable, no matter how correct it is. Catalogs solve discovery the same way search engines solved the web — by indexing metadata, not the data itself.

slides.markdown:
A warehouse with ten thousand tables has a discovery problem baked into its scale: even a perfectly correct, well-governed dataset is useless to someone who doesn't know it exists, doesn't know what it means, or doesn't trust it enough to build on.

A **data catalog** is the index that solves this — schema, ownership, description, usage, and [lineage](data-lineage), all in one searchable place, so "is there a table for this" and "can I trust it" both have fast, reliable answers instead of requiring someone to already know who to ask.

At small scale, discovery is a Slack message — "does anyone have customer data?" and someone answers. That doesn't survive scale: a large organization can have thousands of tables across dozens of teams, and no single person knows what all of them are for, whether they're still maintained, or whether the numbers in them can be trusted.

The practical failure mode this produces isn't "can't find data" — it's worse: people rebuild the same dataset from scratch because they didn't know an existing, better-maintained version already existed, or they build on a table that was quietly deprecated months ago and nobody updates them because nobody knew they depended on it.

A useful catalog entry for a dataset holds several distinct kinds of metadata, each answering a different question a first-time user has: **schema** (what columns exist, what types), **owner** (who built and maintains this — the concrete answer to "who do I ask"), **description** (what is this table *for*, in plain language, not just its column list), **tags** (searchable categorization — "PII," "finance," "deprecated"), **usage stats** (how often is this actually queried, by whom — a strong trust signal on its own), and **lineage** (where did this come from, what depends on it).

No single field answers "can I trust this table" on its own — it's the combination that lets someone form a real judgment in seconds instead of guessing.

A catalog's whole value depends on indexing across every place data actually lives, not just one system — a warehouse, a data lake, and a BI tool's own saved definitions all get pulled into one searchable index, so a user doesn't need to know *which* system holds what they're looking for before they can search for it.

slides.subTitle: Who to ask, who gets paged
slides.markdown:
"Owner" sounds like a formality, but it's often the single most-used field in a catalog, because it answers the question every investigation eventually needs answered: who actually knows this table well enough to help, and who should be paged if it breaks.

Without a recorded owner, finding the right person is itself a multi-step search — check who last edited the pipeline code, ask around, hope someone remembers. With ownership recorded as metadata, it's a lookup: one field, answered instantly, every time, regardless of how much organizational turnover has happened since the table was first built.

slides.sectionTitle: A catalog populated once and never updated
slides.markdown:
A common launch pattern: a team runs a big initiative to document every table in the catalog, gets to 90% coverage, celebrates, and moves on. Eighteen months later, half the descriptions describe a table's *old* structure, several "owners" left the company or the team a year ago, and half the newly created tables since launch were never entered at all.

This is worse than having no catalog, for the same reason a stale lineage diagram is worse than no diagram: it still looks authoritative, so people trust an owner field that points at someone who left, or a description that no longer matches the actual schema, and make decisions based on information that's confidently wrong rather than visibly absent. A catalog's value depends entirely on it staying current, which means metadata maintenance has to be a continuous process, not a one-time initiative with a finish line.

| | Automated metadata harvesting | Manual curation |
|---|---|---|
| What it captures | Schema, column types, row counts, query frequency — anything derivable from the system itself | Descriptions, business context, ownership intent, "what is this actually for" |
| Staleness risk | Low — refreshed automatically on a schedule or on change | High — depends on someone remembering to update it |
| Coverage | Complete, by construction — every table gets basic metadata for free | Partial — depends on someone actually doing the work |
| What it can't provide | The *meaning* behind a column, or why a table exists | Real understanding, but only where someone invested the effort |

The two are complementary, not competing: automated harvesting guarantees a baseline for everything; manual curation adds the human judgment automated tools structurally can't produce, wherever someone bothers to add it.

slides.subTitle: Tying a column to the term the business uses
slides.markdown:
A column is named `is_active_30d` in the schema. The business calls the same concept "active user." A **business glossary** is the explicit mapping between the two — a small, curated dictionary of business terms, each linked to the actual technical columns that implement it.

Without this mapping, a new analyst searching a catalog for "active user" might not find `is_active_30d` at all, because the search only matches technical names. With a glossary entry connecting the two, the business term becomes a real search path into the technical catalog, and — just as importantly — it's a natural place to record which definition is the "official" one when [multiple candidate definitions](semantic-metrics-layer) exist across the organization.

A junior answer to "why do we need a catalog" is "so people can search for tables." A senior answer names the actual failure being prevented: without a trustworthy catalog, organizations pay a repeated tax of rebuilt-from-scratch duplicate datasets, silently broken dependencies on deprecated tables, and hours lost per investigation just finding the right person to ask.

And critically, a senior answer treats "we built a catalog" and "the catalog stays accurate" as two separate problems — the second one is the harder, ongoing half of the work, and it's the half most initiatives underinvest in.

A catalog makes data discoverable. It doesn't, on its own, control who's allowed to see what — that's a distinct concern the next topic covers directly: classifying sensitive data, enforcing row- and column-level access, and the compliance obligations that shape how pipelines handle personal data in the first place.
